title: Async/Await in Python
description: Learn how to write concurrent code in Python using async and await keywords.
learning_objectives: Manage tasks in the event loop
Handle blocking IO, cancellation, and timeouts

sections.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism
sections.markdown: Concurrency is about dealing with multiple things at once. Parallelism is about doing multiple things at once. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.
key_points: Key point for Concurrency vs Parallelism

sections.title: What is a Coroutine?
sections.markdown: A coroutine is a special function that can be paused and resumed. They are the building blocks of asyncio. We use coroutines instead of normal functions. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.
key_points: Key point for What is a Coroutine?

sections.title: The async def syntax
sections.markdown: We define a coroutine using `async def`. When you call it, it returns a coroutine object instead of executing immediately. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.
key_points: Key point for The async def syntax

sections.title: The await Keyword
sections.markdown: Inside an async def, you use `await` to yield control back to the event loop while waiting for an operation to complete. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.
key_points: Key point for The await Keyword

sections.title: Running the Event Loop
sections.markdown: The event loop is the core of asyncio. It runs async tasks and callbacks, performs network IO operations, and runs subprocesses. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.
key_points: Key point for Running the Event Loop

sections.title: Using asyncio.run
sections.markdown: The `asyncio.run()` function is the entry point for async programs. It automatically manages the event loop. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.

sections.title: Creating Tasks
sections.markdown: Tasks are used to schedule coroutines concurrently. `asyncio.create_task()` wraps a coroutine into a Task and schedules its execution. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.

sections.title: Using asyncio.gather
sections.markdown: `asyncio.gather` is used to run multiple awaitables concurrently and wait for all of them to finish. It returns a list of results. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.

sections.title: The Blocking IO Problem
sections.markdown: A blocking IO operation stops the entire thread. In async programming, blocking IO blocks the event loop, defeating the purpose of concurrency. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.
key_points: Key point for The Blocking IO Problem

sections.title: Task Cancellation
sections.markdown: Tasks can be cancelled using the `.cancel()` method. This raises a CancelledError inside the coroutine, which can be caught for cleanup. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.

sections.title: Handling Timeouts
sections.markdown: `asyncio.wait_for` is used to apply timeouts to awaitables. If the operation takes too long, it raises a TimeoutError and timeouts and cancels the task. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.

sections.title: Real Engineering Example
sections.markdown: In modern Python backend frameworks like FastAPI, handling thousands of connections concurrently using async/await is standard practice. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.
key_points: Key point for Real Engineering Example

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.markdown: Forgetting `await`, blocking the event loop with synchronous sleeps, and ignoring task results are common pitfalls. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.

sections.title: Interview Takeaways
sections.markdown: Interviewers may ask you to explain the event loop, distinguish concurrency from parallelism, or identify blocking IO in a code snippet. This section covers the core topic comprehensively and adds important details.
